context: The opening verb of the Bible — 'In the beginning God created' — and a word reserved exclusively for divine action throughout the Hebrew scriptures.
definition: A Hebrew verb used only with God as its subject, distinguishing divine creation from human making or crafting. Unlike other Hebrew words for making (asah, yatsar), bara carries the sense of bringing forth something entirely new, often out of nothing. Its exclusive divine subject is theologically significant.
significance: Because bara is never used of human activity, it marks a categorical distinction between Creator and creature. When David prays 'Create in me a clean heart,' he uses this word — asking for the kind of new beginning only God can bring about.

context: The word of the Lord came to the prophets; events in Israel's history were called dĕbarim — words and things at once.
definition: A remarkable Hebrew noun that means both word and thing simultaneously — a linguistic fact that reflects the Hebrew conviction that speech is not merely descriptive but creative and effective. The phrase debar YHWH, the word of the LORD, drives the prophetic books from first to last.
significance: That the same word means both 'word' and 'event' says something profound: in biblical thought, divine speech is not commentary on reality but the engine of it. What God says, happens. The creation narrative shows this — God speaks, and there is light.

context: One of the great ethical terms of the prophets — what the Lord requires and what Israel repeatedly failed to practice.
definition: From the verb shaphat, to judge or govern. Mishpat carries the full range of judicial and ethical meaning: a legal decision, an ordinance, the act of judging rightly, and the state of justice as a social reality. The prophets use it in tandem with tzedakah (righteousness) as the twin pillars of the just society God demands.
significance: Mishpat is not only about courtrooms — it is about the ordering of communal life so that the poor, the widow, the orphan, and the alien receive what is due them. Where mishpat is absent, the prophets say, no amount of religious observance is acceptable to God.

context: The Hebrew word for prophet — one who speaks on behalf of another, specifically the one who speaks for God to the people.
definition: Likely from a root meaning to call or to announce. A nabi is fundamentally a spokesperson — the one sent by God to declare the divine word. The office is distinct from that of priest or king and often stands in tension with both. Plural: nebi'im, the Prophets, the second division of the Hebrew canon.
significance: The nabi does not primarily predict the future — the prophet's first task is to confront the present. Israel's prophets spoke judgment into comfortable religion, comfort into despair, and always did so because they had heard a word they could not stay silent about.

translation: holiness, that which is set apart
context: The dominant category of Israel's ritual and moral life — applied to God, the Temple, the Sabbath, and the people themselves.
definition: From a root meaning to cut off, separate, or set apart. Qodesh names the fundamental characteristic of God — his absolute otherness — and, derivatively, everything consecrated to him. The Holy of Holies is qodesh haqqodashim: the set-apart of the set-apart. Israel was called to be a goy qadosh, a holy nation.
significance: Holiness in scripture is not primarily about moral purity but about divine otherness — the uncrossable distance between the Creator and his creation. The dramatic arc of redemption is that this terrifying holiness does not consume the sinner but, in Christ, comes near.

context: The deep, visceral compassion — often used in the plural to intensify the emotion — that God is said to have for his people.
definition: A plural noun from rechem, meaning womb. Rachamim names the deep, bodily love a mother has for her child — mercy that is as physical and involuntary as a heartbeat. When God is said to have rachamim, the image is maternal, organic, and overwhelming. The singular racham is often translated 'compassion' or 'mercy.'
significance: That the Hebrew word for compassion is rooted in the word for womb tells us everything about its character. God's mercy is not a policy decision but something like a mother's ache for her child — a feeling that cannot be reasoned away. The Book of Lamentations clings to this truth amid ruins.

context: The instrument blown at Sinai, before the walls of Jericho, at the Day of Atonement, and anticipated at the last day.
definition: A wind instrument made from a ram's horn, used throughout Israel's history for public proclamation: mustering armies, marking feast days, announcing the jubilee year, and signaling the presence of God. Its sound is described as tekiah (a long blast) or shevarim (broken blasts), each carrying specific liturgical meaning.
significance: The shofar marks the boundary between the ordinary and the momentous. At Sinai it announced the arrival of God; before Jericho it accompanied the power of obedient faith; at the New Year (Rosh Hashanah) it awakens the soul to repentance. Paul heard its echo in the last trumpet that will announce the resurrection.

context: A verb at the heart of Israel's covenant faith — God remembers his people, and Israel is commanded to remember what God has done.
definition: The Hebrew word for memory carries a force that English underestimates. To zakar is not simply to recall mentally but to act on what is recalled — God 'remembering' Noah meant God moving to rescue him. Israel's call to remember the Exodus means re-entering it as if present. Memory, in Hebrew, is not passive.
significance: Because Israel's faith is rooted in history, memory is a theological act. The Passover, the Sabbath, the Psalms — all are structures of communal remembrance. Jesus's words at the Last Supper, 'Do this in remembrance of me,' place the Eucharist inside this tradition: active, covenant-binding memory.

context: The most common Hebrew word for love — used of God's love for Israel, of human love for God, and of romantic love in the Song of Solomon.
definition: From the verb ahav, to love. Ahavah encompasses a broad range of love: romantic desire (Song of Solomon), familial devotion (Abraham's love for Isaac), and the covenant love God bears his people. Unlike hesed, which emphasizes loyalty and obligation, ahavah leans toward warm personal feeling and desire.
significance: When Deuteronomy commands Israel to love God with all the heart, it uses ahavah — the same word as romantic love. The prophets, especially Hosea, use marital imagery to describe God's relationship with Israel, with ahavah as the love betrayed by idolatry and renewed in grace.

context: The intermediary between God and Israel — the one who offered sacrifice, maintained the sanctuary, and pronounced the blessing.
definition: The Hebrew word for priest, applied to those consecrated for the service of the sanctuary. Kohanim were drawn from the tribe of Levi, specifically from the line of Aaron. Their role was threefold: to offer sacrifice on Israel's behalf, to maintain and guard the holy space, and to teach Torah and pronounce the priestly blessing.
significance: The Letter to the Hebrews presents Christ as the final and definitive kohen — a high priest after the order of Melchizedek who has passed through the heavens and whose one sacrifice renders all others complete. The old priesthood was scaffolding; the new high priest is what the scaffolding was holding up.

context: The same Hebrew word describes both human messengers and the heavenly beings sent by God — the distinction is context, not vocabulary.
definition: From a root meaning to send on a mission. A malak is simply a sent one — a messenger. Context determines whether the messenger is human (a royal envoy) or heavenly (a divine emissary). The malak YHWH, the angel of the LORD, appears at critical junctures in the narrative, often speaking as if he were God himself.
significance: The angel of the LORD in the Old Testament is a figure of enduring theological interest — speaking divine first-person speech, accepting worship, yet distinct from God. Many in the Christian tradition have read these appearances as pre-incarnate encounters with the Son. Whether or not, they establish that God's messengers are not background figures but bearers of his very presence.

context: The word that describes Israel's bondage in Egypt, Moses's relationship to God, and the suffering Servant of Isaiah.
definition: Eved covers the full spectrum from chattel slavery to voluntary, honored service. The great figures of faith are called eved YHWH — servant of the LORD — as a title of distinction. Isaiah's four Servant Songs describe a mysterious figure who bears Israel's calling, suffers vicariously, and is vindicated by God.
significance: That God's greatest figures — Abraham, Moses, David — are called his servants, and that the Messiah himself takes the form of a servant, inverts every human hierarchy. Paul sees Christ's kenosis — his self-emptying as eved — as the pattern for all Christian community: to have the mind of the one who became a slave.

context: The Hebrew seat of thought, will, and emotion — not sentiment alone but the entire inner life of a person.
definition: The Hebrew lev (also levav) corresponds not to the emotional heart of English usage but to the whole interior life: what one thinks, wills, intends, and feels. To love God with the whole lev is to orient every faculty toward him. The hardening of Pharaoh's lev is the hardening of his will and reason, not just his emotions.
significance: Ezekiel's promise of a new heart — lev hadash — is one of the great covenant promises of the Old Testament. The old heart of stone, set against God, will be replaced by a heart of flesh, soft and responsive to his Spirit. The New Testament presents this as fulfilled in the indwelling of the Holy Spirit.

context: The 'hand of God' or 'mighty hand of God' is one of the most common images in the Hebrew Bible for divine power in action.
definition: The primary Hebrew word for hand, frequently extended metaphorically to mean power, authority, and agency. The phrase yad chazakah, the strong hand, describes God's act of deliverance in the Exodus. The hand of the LORD coming upon the prophets signals the onset of prophetic vision or overwhelming presence.
significance: The yad YHWH is not mere metaphor — it names the specific, historical intervention of God in the world. When Israel remembered the Exodus they remembered a strong hand and an outstretched arm. The incarnation, for the early Christians, was the ultimate reaching of that hand into human flesh.

context: The Old Testament's word for repentance — not primarily an inner feeling but a physical turning around, a change of direction.
definition: A verb meaning to turn, to return, to come back. The prophetic call to repentance is shubah, return — often addressed to a people who have turned away from God and are called to reverse course. It is a spatial metaphor: sin is movement away from God; repentance is the turn that heads home.
significance: Israel's prophets nearly all use shub as their fundamental call. What is remarkable is that the turning is possible at all — it is not earned or achieved but offered. The father in Luke 15 runs toward the returning son while he is still far off, dramatizing what shub looks like from God's side.

context: Used of Israel's greatest warriors, of the divine name 'Mighty God,' and of the expected Messiah.
definition: From the root gabar, to be strong, to prevail. Gibor names a man of outstanding strength, courage, or valor — a warrior, a champion. David's elite soldiers are called his giborim. But the term is also applied to God himself: El Gibor, Mighty God, one of Isaiah's names for the coming ruler whose shoulders will bear the government.
significance: Israel's kings were valued for military might, and the Messiah's names in Isaiah 9 include El Gibor — Mighty God. The paradox of the New Testament is that this divine warrior came not with sword but with a towel, and won the greatest battle through a cross. The power of God, Paul says, looks like weakness to the world.

context: The same Hebrew word covers labor, ritual service, and worship — the Bible does not sharply distinguish them.
definition: From the verb avad (the same root as eved). Avodah names work in its broadest sense: agricultural labor, the service of the Levites and priests in the Temple, and the worship of God. Its range insists that there is no sacred/secular divide at the root of Hebrew thought — all faithful work is service, and all worship is work.
significance: Paul's call to offer our bodies as a living sacrifice, our 'spiritual worship,' uses a Greek word (latreia) that translates precisely this Hebrew avodah. The blurring of work and worship is not an accident of biblical language — it is the theology. To tend a garden or serve a neighbor is to perform avodah before God.

context: The blessing passed from God to his people and through his people to the world — the great thread of the covenant narrative.
definition: From the root barak, to bless, related to the word for knee — suggesting a bowing, a gift given from a position of generosity. A berakah is the concrete good that flows from a blessing: favor, fruitfulness, prosperity, peace. The Aaronic blessing is a berakah; the promises to Abraham are a berakah for all nations.
significance: The biblical story can be read as the journey of the berakah: God blesses Abraham so that all families of the earth might be blessed. Paul tells the Ephesians they are blessed with every spiritual blessing in Christ — the full weight of the promise arriving at last in the Messiah.

context: The word that describes the daily offerings of the Temple — the continual burnt offering that kept the fire on the altar never going out.
definition: An adverb and adjective meaning always, continually, without cessation. In the priestly legislation, the tamid is the 'regular offering' — a lamb offered morning and evening every day without exception. It names a rhythm of worship that is unbroken, day after day, as the pulse of Israel's life before God.
significance: The tamid offering structured Israel's days the way morning and evening prayer would later structure monastic life — an unbroken offering before God. Hebrews interprets Christ's intercession using this imagery: he lives to make intercession tamid, always and without ceasing, as the sacrifice that never needs repeating.

context: The Hebrew word for God's covenant people — more intimate than goy (nation), carrying the sense of family and kinship.
definition: The primary Hebrew word for a people as a community of common origin or covenant relationship. Whereas goy often applies to foreign nations, am carries a warmth of solidarity: am YHWH, the people of the LORD. The phrase am segulah, treasured people, expresses Israel's unique covenant standing.
significance: Peter borrows Exodus and Deuteronomy's language wholesale to address the church: 'You are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation.' The identity God carved out for Israel — am, people, kin — is extended in the New Testament to all who are in Christ, Jew and Gentile together.

translation: truth, reality, that which is unconcealed
context: The Greek word behind Jesus's 'I am the way and the truth and the life,' carrying philosophical depth the English translation barely hints at.
definition: From a-letheia — literally 'un-hiddenness' or 'not-forgetting.' Greek philosophers used it for the nature of reality disclosed when illusion is stripped away. In the New Testament it takes on covenantal overtones from the Hebrew emet, naming not just correct propositions but the trustworthy faithfulness of God and the full reality of what is in Christ.
significance: When Pilate asks 'What is truth?' and the answer is standing right in front of him, John is making a point as much philosophical as spiritual. In Christ, aletheia has a face — truth is not a system but a person. To know the truth, in John's Gospel, is to know Jesus.

context: The Greek word for resurrection — the bodily rising from the dead that is the cornerstone of the Christian proclamation.
definition: From ana (up) and histemi (to stand). Anastasis means a standing up, a rising. In the New Testament it becomes the technical term for the bodily resurrection of the dead — the reversal of death that happened to Jesus and is promised to all who are in him. Anastasis is never a merely spiritual concept in the New Testament; it always carries bodily overtones.
significance: Paul tells the Corinthians that if there is no anastasis, their faith is empty and they are still in their sins. The resurrection is not an optional metaphor for the early Christians — it is the hinge of history, the event that makes every other claim possible. To preach the gospel is to preach anastasis.

context: The word describing John's river practice and the rite instituted by Jesus as the entry point into the Christian community.
definition: From an older verb bapto, to dip or plunge. Baptizo means to immerse in a liquid, to dye by soaking, or to overwhelm. The practice John brought to the Jordan and Jesus commanded at his ascension carries this physical image: going under and coming up — death and resurrection enacted in water.
significance: Paul reads baptism as enacted theology: going down into the water is burial with Christ, coming up is resurrection. The act says in water what the creed says in words. That the verb specifically means to immerse — not merely to sprinkle — underscores the totality of what is claimed: nothing held back, wholly submerged in Christ.

context: The power at work in the miracles of Jesus, the resurrection, and the coming of the Spirit at Pentecost.
definition: The Greek word for power in the sense of inherent ability, force, or capacity. In the New Testament it refers to miraculous works (the dunameis, mighty works, of Jesus), the power of the resurrection, and above all the power of the Holy Spirit given to the church. English 'dynamic' and 'dynamite' come from this root.
significance: Paul's claim that the gospel is the dunamis of God for salvation overturns expectations at every level. Rome had dunamis — armies, legions, the power to crucify. God's power looks like a crucified Jew and an empty tomb. The Spirit's dunamis does not coerce but transforms — from the inside, one person at a time.

context: The word translated 'gospel' — the good news about Jesus that the first Christians announced as a world-altering proclamation.
definition: From eu (good) and angelos (messenger) — literally, a good message or good news. In the Greco-Roman world it was used for imperial announcements of victory, accession, or peace. The early Christians borrowed this public, political term and applied it to Jesus — their emperor had a better euangelion, one that outlasted Rome.
significance: Calling the story of Jesus a euangelion was an act of political audacity in the Roman Empire. Caesar's birth, victories, and decrees were announced as good news. To proclaim a different euangelion — one centered on a crucified provincial — was to plant a flag of rival allegiance that the Empire eventually understood as subversive.

context: The Greek equivalent of Hebrew qodesh — used of God, of sacred things, and (remarkably) as the standard New Testament word for ordinary believers.
definition: The Greek adjective for holy or set apart, corresponding directly to the Hebrew qodesh. In the Septuagint it translates qodesh throughout. In the New Testament, hagioi — holy ones, saints — is Paul's ordinary term for Christian believers. Not a superlative few but the standard description of the community in Christ.
significance: That Paul addresses his letters to the hagioi in Rome or Corinth — communities with very visible failures — is deliberately provocative. Holiness is not first an achievement but a status conferred by the Holy One. The task is then to become in life what you already are in Christ.

context: The word describing the life of the early Jerusalem community and the shared participation in Christ that makes the church more than a club.
definition: From koinos, common. Koinonia names a sharing in common — whether of material goods, of suffering, of joy, or of participation in someone's life. In the New Testament it describes the Jerusalem church's sharing of possessions, partnership in the gospel, the Lord's Supper as communion, and the believer's participation in the life of Christ himself.
significance: Koinonia is not mere socializing. Paul uses it to describe the Lord's Supper as a participation — a real sharing in — the body and blood of Christ. The community that gathers around this table is constituted by a common life that runs deeper than friendship: it is a sharing in the divine life itself.

context: The first word of both John the Baptist's and Jesus's public preaching, often flattened into mere emotional regret.
definition: From meta (after, beyond, change) and nous (mind). Metanoia is a profound reorientation of the entire person — a change of mind that is also a change of direction. It goes beyond guilt or remorse to a new way of seeing and therefore a new way of living. The English word 'repentance' (from Latin poenitentia, penalty) unfortunately leans toward punishment rather than transformation.
significance: Jesus's first sermon word is metanoia — not a call to try harder but a call to see differently. The kingdom of heaven changes what is visible. Those who perceive it differently will live differently. Metanoia is what happens when you see that everything has changed and recalibrate your whole life accordingly.

context: The Greek word that translates Hebrew kavod — used of God's manifest presence, of the honor due to persons, and of the final transformation of believers.
definition: Originally the Greek word for opinion or reputation — what others think of you. In the Septuagint it translates Hebrew kavod (weight, glory), shifting its meaning entirely toward objective divine splendor. In the New Testament doxa names the radiant, overwhelming presence of God, the honor of Christ at his resurrection, and the future state awaiting believers.
significance: John says the Word became flesh and they beheld his doxa — the divine glory dwelling in a human body. Paul says believers are being transformed from doxa to doxa into the same image. The story of creation and redemption is, among other things, the story of divine glory seeking to fill the earth through a renewed humanity.

context: Distinct from bios (biological life) in the New Testament — zoe names the life of the age to come, the life that is in God, the life Christ came to give.
definition: Greek has several words for life; zoe in the New Testament is specifically elevated to name the life that belongs to God and is given through Christ. John's Gospel uses it 36 times — zoe aionios, eternal life, is not simply life that goes on forever but life of a qualitatively different order, beginning now.
significance: Jesus says he came that they might have zoe, and have it abundantly. This is not a promise of longevity but of a share in the life that belongs to God. The Gospel of John identifies Jesus himself as the zoe — not a teacher of life but the life itself, such that to have him is to have life, and to be without him is death regardless of biological status.

context: The verb behind 'salvation' — a word the New Testament applies to healing, rescue from danger, and eternal redemption without distinguishing sharply between them.
definition: To save, rescue, preserve, heal, or make whole. In the Gospels it describes Jesus healing the sick, and the same word — 'your faith has saved you' — is spoken both to the woman healed of a hemorrhage and to the sinners whose sins are forgiven. The breadth is deliberate: sozo names a total rescue of the whole person.
significance: The narrowing of sozo to mean only 'spiritual salvation' loses something the New Testament insists on. Jesus healed bodies, fed crowds, calmed storms — and all of it is the saving work of the one whose name means 'YHWH saves.' The full scope of redemption is physical, social, and cosmic, not only spiritual.

context: The standard Greek word for God, used in the Septuagint to translate Elohim and adopted wholesale by the New Testament.
definition: The primary Greek word for deity or divinity. In pagan usage it could apply to any god; the Septuagint and New Testament restrict it overwhelmingly to the God of Israel. John's prologue uses it with precision: the Word was with ton theon (the God, with the article, the Father) and the Word was theos (God in nature, without article) — a distinction that drove centuries of theological reflection.
significance: Thomas's confession in John 20 — 'My Lord and my God' — is the climax of the Gospel: a Jewish monotheist addressing the risen Jesus with the word theos. The New Testament's high Christology is not a later development but present from the first generation, in the mouths of those who knew him.

context: The Septuagint's translation of YHWH, and the word the earliest Christian confession — 'Jesus is Lord' — applied to Christ.
definition: The Greek word for lord, master, or owner — one who has authority and to whom others are accountable. In the Septuagint it translates the divine name YHWH throughout the Old Testament. The earliest Christian confession, kurios Iesous (Jesus is Lord), was therefore a staggering claim: this person bears the divine name.
significance: When Caesar's subjects said 'Caesar is Lord' (kurios Kaisar), and Christians said 'Jesus is Lord' (kurios Iesous), both parties understood the claim. The one Lord of Israel and the cosmos is not Caesar but the crucified and risen Jesus. The confession was not private piety — it was public allegiance with political consequences.

context: The Greek counterpart to Hebrew lev — the whole inner life of a person, seat of thought and decision, not merely emotion.
definition: Like Hebrew lev, kardia in the New Testament is not primarily emotional but volitional and cognitive — the center of the human person's inner life, including mind, will, memory, and feeling. Jesus says it is from the kardia that evil thoughts proceed; Paul prays that Christ might dwell in the kardia of the Ephesians.
significance: The reduction of the heart to mere sentiment is foreign to both testaments. When God writes his law on the kardia (as promised in Jeremiah and enacted in the New Covenant), the whole person is being claimed and reformed — not just the feelings but the will, the memory, and the habits of thought.

context: A complex New Testament word ranging from the neutral 'body' to the deeply loaded 'fallen human nature in opposition to the Spirit.'
definition: The Greek word for flesh, physical substance, or the body as mortal and creaturely. In John's Gospel sarx is used neutrally — the Word became sarx (flesh). In Paul it becomes more complex: sarx can mean simply the physical body, or it can name the fallen, sin-oriented human nature that stands in opposition to the Spirit of God.
significance: John's audacity is that the Word became sarx — the divine took on the very stuff that Paul associates with human weakness and sin-orientation. The incarnation dignifies the physical even as Paul names the sinful tendency of unaided human nature. Sarx is not the body as evil, but the body as it is apart from the renewing Spirit.

context: The word for 'end' that means not termination but completion — the goal toward which something moves.
definition: From the root tel-, to achieve or accomplish. Telos names the completion of something, its perfection, the goal toward which a thing is aimed. Jesus's final word on the cross in John — tetelestai, 'it is finished/accomplished' — is from this root: not 'it is over' but 'it is complete.' Aristotle used telos to describe the proper end of a thing — what it fully is when fully realized.
significance: Paul says Christ is the telos of the Torah — its goal, its completion, the one it was always pointing toward. When Jesus cries tetelestai, he is not announcing defeat but achievement: the mission is accomplished, the sacrifice accepted, the redemption complete. The cross is a telos, not a terminus.

context: A theologically precise word describing how Christ's death deals with the problem of sin before a holy God.
definition: From the verb hilaskomai — to appease, to make propitious, to atone. Hilasmos names the act or means by which divine wrath against sin is satisfied and the relationship between God and humanity is restored. In the Septuagint the related hilasterion translates the Hebrew kapporeth — the mercy seat, the lid of the ark where the blood of atonement was sprinkled.
significance: John says Jesus is the hilasmos for our sins, and not only ours but for the whole world. The word insists that the cross is not only a moral example but an objective act: the holy wrath of God against all that destroys his creation has been met, borne, and exhausted in the Son. Love and justice embrace at the cross.

context: The root of the English word 'deacon' — service in the New Testament ranges from waiting on tables to the apostolic ministry of the word.
definition: Service rendered for the benefit of another, particularly practical, hands-on ministry. The word carries connotations of waiting on tables and meeting practical needs — not prestigious service but humble, concrete care. Paradoxically the New Testament applies it both to the humble service of the poor and to the highest apostolic calling.
significance: When the apostles distinguish between the diakonia of the word and the diakonia of tables, they do not rank them — both are service, both are ministry. Paul applies the same word to his apostolic calling that Luke uses for the widows' food distribution. In Christ's kingdom, serving at table and preaching the gospel are not separate categories.

context: The standard New Testament word for prayer — appearing dozens of times as both the act itself and occasionally the place where it happens.
definition: From pros (toward) and euchomai (to wish, to pray) — literally, prayer oriented toward God. It is the most general and comprehensive Greek word for prayer in the New Testament, covering petition, intercession, thanksgiving, and worship. Jewish communities sometimes called their meeting places proseuchai — houses of prayer.
significance: Jesus quotes Isaiah calling the Temple a 'house of proseuche for all nations.' The scope of prayer in the New Testament is vast: Paul commands proseuche with thanksgiving in everything, in all circumstances. It is not a technique but a posture — the continuous orientation of one's whole life toward God.

context: Jesus's own title for the Holy Spirit in John's Gospel — the one he promises to send when he goes.
definition: From para (alongside) and kaleo (to call) — one called alongside to help. In the legal world a parakletos was a defense advocate. Jesus uses it for the Holy Spirit in John 14–16, promising that this Advocate will teach, remind, convict, and lead the disciples into all truth after his departure. John also applies the title to Jesus himself in 1 John 2:1.
significance: The Parakletos is not a consolation prize for Christ's absence — Jesus says it is to the disciples' advantage that he goes, so that the Parakletos can come. The Spirit does not represent an absent Christ; the Spirit is the mode in which the risen Christ remains present — inside the community, inside the believer, teaching, guiding, and interceding.
